# How to Summarize a Long YouTube Video in 60 Seconds with Any AI

> **In short:** Paste a YouTube link into any AI assistant and ask for a summary — in about a minute you get the main points, key quotes, and a one-sentence takeaway without watching. The catch: not every assistant reads YouTube links directly, so we cover that fallback too.

Found a one-hour interview you don't have time to watch? A 40-minute lecture you need for work tomorrow? You don't have to skip it. Any modern AI assistant can read the page a YouTube link points to and pull out the important parts. Here's the whole workflow, start to finish.

## Before you start
- **A YouTube link** — the URL of the video you want summarized. It works on desktop, mobile, or in the YouTube app.
- **An AI assistant** you already have access to — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or any other mainstream option. Free or paid plans both work, though some assistants may need a paid plan to read external links reliably.
- **Roughly 2–3 minutes** for the whole thing, including reading the summary.

## Step 1 — Copy the YouTube video link
Open the YouTube video you want summarized and look at the address bar at the top of your browser (or the link shown under the video title in the YouTube app). A YouTube link starts with **youtube.com** or **youtu.be** and ends with a jumble of letters and numbers — that's the video's unique ID. Tap and hold (on phone) or click and drag (on computer) to highlight the whole address, then copy it. On the YouTube mobile app, tap **Share** under the video and choose **Copy link** instead — it's faster. If you're on a TV or game console and don't see a copy option, open the video in a phone or computer browser to grab the link from there.
💬 Example: Your copied link will look something like youtube.com/watch?v=AbCdEfGh123 — the letters and numbers at the end are the video's ID.
You'll know it worked when the address is highlighted or your phone briefly says "Copied."

## Step 2 — Open your AI assistant
Open the website or app for the AI you normally use. Most readers already have at least one of these: ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, or Le Chat. Open a new chat — look for a button like **New chat**, **New conversation**, or a **+** or pencil icon in the corner of the screen. Starting fresh matters because a long previous chat can confuse the assistant about what you want right now.
You'll know it worked when you see an empty message box, usually at the bottom of the screen, with a prompt that says something like "Message…" or "Ask anything" — your exact wording may be different.

## Step 3 — Paste the link and ask for a summary
Click in the empty message box and paste the YouTube link you copied. Then type your request. A short, clear instruction works best — tell the assistant what you want and how long the answer should be. Press **Enter** (or tap the send arrow). The assistant will fetch the video's public page, read its title and description, and (on most assistants) the transcript too. A short summary appears in under a minute.
💬 Example: "Here's a YouTube link: [paste your link]. Summarize this video in 5 bullet points and keep it under 150 words."
You'll know it worked when the assistant replies with bullet points or a short paragraph that names the video's main topic and the people or ideas involved.

## Step 4 — Pull out a few key quotes
The summary gives you the gist, but sometimes you want the actual words someone said — a striking line, a statistic, or a memorable phrase. Ask for those next. Quotes are useful when you want to share the video with a friend or quote it in your own work. Type a follow-up question that specifically asks for verbatim lines. The assistant will return them with quotation marks and usually say who said them.
💬 Example: "Now pull out 3 key quotes from that video, with the speaker's name for each one. Keep each quote to one sentence."
You'll know it worked when the reply contains lines wrapped in quotation marks and the speaker is named beside each one.

## Step 5 — Get a one-sentence takeaway
A bullet-point summary is great for studying, but a single sentence is easier to remember and share. Ask for the takeaway last. The assistant will compress everything it just read into one line you can use as a reference or send to a colleague. If you have a specific audience in mind — your team, your teacher, your family — say so, because the assistant will word the takeaway differently for each.
💬 Example: "In one sentence, what's the single most important takeaway from that video, written so I can send it to my manager?"
You'll know it worked when the reply is a single complete sentence (not a paragraph) that captures the main idea.

## Step 6 — Save or share your summary
Now that you have the points, quotes, and takeaway, decide where they should live. Most assistants have a **Copy** button at the top or bottom of each reply — tap it to grab the text and paste it into your notes app, email, or document. Some assistants also have a **Share** button that creates a link you can send to someone. If you don't see either button, you can manually select the text and copy it the same way you copied the YouTube link in Step 1.
You'll know it worked when the summary text is sitting in another app — your notes, an email draft, or a message — and you can read it again without opening the AI chat.

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting the link without any instructions.** The assistant may reply with "What would you like me to do with this?" — always tell it you want a summary, in what length, and for whom.
- **Assuming every assistant reads YouTube links directly.** A few assistants only read the video's title and description, not its full transcript. If your summary feels thin or vague, ask the assistant to look up the video's transcript, or copy the transcript yourself from YouTube (look for an option like **Show transcript** under the video description) and paste that text instead of the link.
- **Trusting the summary on a topic you know nothing about.** Summaries are usually accurate, but AI can still mix up names, dates, or numbers. For important decisions — anything medical, legal, financial, or that affects other people — verify the quote or fact by checking the original video yourself.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Next time someone sends you a 30-minute tutorial or a long podcast episode on YouTube, decide in 60 seconds whether it's actually worth your time. Skip the noise, keep the useful stuff.
- **For your business or work:** Before a meeting, paste the link to a recorded presentation or webinar and ask for the five main points plus the speaker's recommendations. You walk in prepared without sitting through the whole recording.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one YouTube video you've been putting off, follow the six steps above, and see how much you actually retain from the summary versus the full video. Most people are surprised how often the bullet points are enough.

## Try it now
Open your AI assistant right now, paste the link to any YouTube video you've been meaning to watch, and type: "Summarize this video in 5 bullet points and pull out 2 short quotes." You'll have a usable summary in about a minute — that's the whole skill.
